T0055.text: All three are counted in ${term("hardset","hard sets")} per muscle per week. Three sets of bench press count as 3 chest sets, and partial credit goes to your front delts and triceps, because they did real work too.

T0056.text: These landmarks come from the volume-landmark framework popularised by Mike Israetel and Renaissance Periodization. They're population averages with wide individual variation, treat them as a starting frame, not a law. Yours may sit higher or lower.

T0058.text: RPE is how hard a set felt, on a 1-10 scale. What it really measures is how many reps you had left.

T0059.text:
RPE 10  → all-out, no reps left
RPE 9   → 1 rep left in the tank
RPE 8   → 2 reps left
RPE 7   → 3 reps left
RPE 6   → 4+ reps left, easy

T0060.text: A target like RPE 8-9 means: pick a weight where you finish the set with about 1-2 reps still in you.

T0061.text: It's the single most useful number you can log. Weight and reps say what you lifted; RPE says how close to your limit it was, which is what actually decides whether the set grew anything.

T0063.text: The least weekly work a muscle needs before it grows at all.

T0064.text: Below MEV you're maintaining at best, even if the sessions feel brutal. Effort doesn't substitute for volume here, a muscle needs a certain amount of total work per week before it has a reason to adapt.

T0065.text: This is the line the Body tab's weak point detection uses. If a muscle sits under its MEV two weeks running, it gets flagged, because that's a muscle you're spending gym time on without getting growth back.

T0067.text: The productive middle, where you get the most growth per set you invest.

T0068.text: Between ${term("mev","MEV")} and MAV is where you want to live most of the time. Adding sets in this range keeps paying off.

T0069.text: Above MAV you're still growing and can still recover, but each extra set returns less than the one before it, so it's a range to use deliberately for a hard block, not to sit in year-round.

T0071.text: The most a muscle can recover from. Past this, sets cost fatigue but stop buying growth.

T0072.text: Going over MRV doesn't just waste the extra sets, it digs a hole. Recovery debt accumulates, your loads on everything else start slipping, and joints and connective tissue take the strain. It usually shows up as strength going backwards while you're working harder than ever.

T0073.text: This is why the ${term("injury","injury risk")} metric weights volume-past-MRV most heavily of all its flags.

T0075.text: A set taken close enough to failure to actually drive growth, roughly ${term("rpe","RPE")} 7 or above.

T0076.text: Warm-ups and easy back-off sets don't count. Research on hypertrophy consistently shows the stimulus falls off sharply once you're more than about 4 reps from failure, so counting every set you performed would badly overstate your real training volume.

T0077.text: Element 26 counts any set with reps logged as a working set, and uses your logged ${term("rpe","RPE")} to judge how hard it was. If you don't log RPE, it assumes a normal hard set (RPE 8) rather than throwing the set away.

T0078.text: Partial credit: a muscle that assists gets a fraction of a set, not a whole one. A bench press pays 1.0 to chest, 0.5 to front delts and 0.5 to triceps. That's why the per-muscle numbers can look odd next to your session total, and why the whole-body tile counts real sets performed instead of summing the columns.

T0083.text: The safe band. Load is progressing at a rate your body can absorb.

T0085.text: A spike. This is the best-established injury marker in sports science, jumping load faster than your tissues adapt is what hurts people, more than the absolute amount.

T0086.text: The practical read: it's not how much you do, it's how fast you changed how much you do. A 1.5× week is how a motivated Monday becomes a strained something on Thursday.

T0087.text: Element 26 needs about four weeks of history before this means anything, so it shows a dash until then.

T0090.text: Element 26 uses the Epley formula: weight × (1 + reps ÷ 30). So 100 lb × 10 reps estimates a 133 lb single.

T0091.text: Why bother: it lets the app compare sets that aren't alike. 100×10 and 115×6 are hard to rank by eye, but as estimated 1RMs (133 vs 138) it's clear the second was stronger. That's how ${term("growth","growth")} and progressive overload get measured when your reps move around week to week.

T0092.text: It's only reliable in the low-rep range, so the calculation caps reps at 12, otherwise a 20-rep set would inflate the estimate wildly.

T0094.text: Training residue that hasn't worn off yet, per muscle, right now.

T0095.text: Every ${term("hardset","hard set")} leaves fatigue behind, and that residue decays over time. Element 26 decays it on an exponential half-life set per muscle: side delts and calves clear in about 36 hours, quads and spinal erectors take 60.

T0096.text: Sets closer to failure leave more behind, an RPE 10 set costs roughly 2.4× what an RPE 6 set does.

T0097.text: Reading the number: 100% means you've just dumped a full ${term("mrv","MRV")} week's worth onto that muscle. Under 20% is fresh. Fatigue is not the same as ${term("recovery","recovery")}, see that entry for why both exist.

T0099.text: How far through its own recovery window a muscle is since the last time you trained it.

T0100.text: Each muscle has a typical turnaround time, 36 hours for side delts, 60 for quads, and a heavier-than-usual session stretches that window proportionally.

T0101.text: Why this isn't just the inverse of ${term("fatigue","fatigue")}: they answer different questions. A muscle you hammered six days ago is fully recovered and ready to train, but a week of hard work can still leave fatigue residue on the books. One tells you if you can train it today; the other tells you whether the week is catching up with you.

T0102.text: Your sleep and energy logs feed into this. Averaging under 6 hours of sleep drops every muscle's recovery, because sleep debt measurably slows tissue repair, that's not a per-muscle effect, so it shifts them all together.

T0104.text: Is this muscle actually progressing? Last 3 weeks against the 3 weeks before.

T0107.text: Change in total volume, the stimulus signal

T0108.text: 50 means holding steady. Above 65 means strength is genuinely trending up. Below 45 means the last block went backwards.

T0109.text: A stall with adequate volume is a different problem from a stall with too little, which is why weak point detection treats them separately: one needs a change of stimulus, the other needs more sets. Piling on volume to fix a fatigue-driven stall makes it worse.

T0121.text: This is a training-load flag, not medical advice. It can't see your sleep quality, your joints, your technique or your history, and it can't predict an injury. Actual pain beats anything on this screen: if something hurts, treat that as the signal.

T0123.text: Giving your body slightly more to handle than last time. It's the one rule that makes training work.

T0124.text: Muscles adapt to what you ask of them. Ask the same thing every week and there's no reason to change. The load has to creep up.

T0125.text: "More" doesn't have to mean weight. Any one of these counts:

T0127.text: Same reps, heavier bar, the most obvious lever

T0129.text: Same weight, one extra rep. Usually the easier win

T0131.text: Adds ${term("volume","volume")}, but has a ceiling, see ${term("mrv","MRV")}

T0133.text: Same numbers, cleaner form, slower lowering, less cheating

T0134.text: You only need one of them to move. Element 26 grades this by comparing your best ${term("e1rm","estimated 1RM")} on each exercise against the last time you did that workout.

T0135.text: Progress is not linear. Beating every lift every week is not the standard, holding steady is fine, and going backwards for a week usually means fatigue, not failure.

T0137.text: Taking a set until you physically cannot complete another rep with good form.

T0138.text: That's ${term("rpe","RPE")} 10. One rep short is RPE 9, two short is RPE 8, that gap is sometimes called reps in reserve.

T0139.text: Failure is a tool, not a target. Sets taken to true failure build a little more per set, but they cost disproportionately more recovery and beat up your joints and connective tissue. Doing every set to failure is one of the most common ways people stall.

T0140.text: The usual advice: keep most sets at RPE 8-9, and save actual failure for the last set of an exercise, ideally on machines and cables rather than heavy free weights, where form breaking down is dangerous.

T0142.text: A deliberately easy week, taken so you can come back stronger.

T0143.text: Fatigue accumulates faster than you notice. After several hard weeks it starts masking your actual strength, you're stronger than your lifts suggest, you just can't express it. A deload lets the fatigue drain off so the strength shows up.

T0144.text: The usual recipe: keep the weights, cut the sets by about half, and stop every set well short of ${term("failure","failure")}. Keeping the loads is what preserves the skill and the stimulus; cutting the sets is what buys the recovery.

T0145.text: Signs you need one: strength going backwards across several lifts at once, high ${term("fatigue","fatigue")} with low ${term("recovery","recovery")} everywhere on the Body tab, poor sleep, and no motivation to train.

T0147.text: Two exercises done back to back with no rest between them.

T0148.text: Your ab finisher is one: crunch → leg raise → crunch, straight through. Because there's no rest inside a superset, Element 26 doesn't start the rest stopwatch between those sets and doesn't grade them for ${term("restwindow","rest length")}.

T0149.text: Supersetting two unrelated muscles, say calves and biceps, is close to free time saved. Supersetting the same muscle raises the difficulty a lot and cuts the weight you can use, so it's a tool for finishers rather than main lifts.

T0151.text: Partial reps at the stretched end of the movement, once full reps run out.

T0152.text: When you can't complete another full rep, you keep going through the bottom portion only — the deepest part of a curl, the stretch at the bottom of a fly. The muscle is under load in its lengthened position, which is the part of the range most associated with growth.

T0153.text: They extend a set past the point where it would otherwise end, so they belong on the last set of an exercise rather than on all of them.

T0154.text: Element 26 counts the set as one ${term("hardset","hard set")}. The partials are extra work inside it, not extra sets.

T0156.text: At failure, strip weight and keep going with no rest.

T0157.text: Take the set to failure, immediately cut the load — commonly 20-30% — and rep out again. Repeat for as many drops as the plan asks for.

T0158.text: Log each drop under the set it belongs to. Element 26 counts the whole thing as one ${term("hardset","hard set")}: the drops add tonnage and fatigue, not set count. Counting a triple drop as three sets would overstate your weekly ${term("volume","volume")} against thresholds that were never measured that way.

T0160.text: One hard activation set, then short mini-sets with a few breaths between.

T0161.text: You take an activation set to roughly ${term("rpe","RPE")} 9, rest only 3-5 deep breaths, then do a mini-set of 3-5 reps. Repeat until you can't hit the target reps. The idea is to keep the muscle near the high-effort end of the set without re-doing the easy reps at the start.

T0162.text: Element 26 counts the activation set plus its mini-sets as one ${term("hardset","hard set")}.

T0164.text: Go to failure, rest 15-20 seconds, go again. Repeat.

T0165.text: Close relative of myo-reps, with slightly longer pauses and usually fewer bursts. Same purpose: more near-failure reps out of one load.

T0168.text: One set broken into small bunches with a planned pause between each.

T0169.text: Unlike the others here, a plan that prescribes clusters normally means every set, not just the last, so Element 26 applies it to all of them.

T0170.text: Counted as one ${term("hardset","hard set")} per cluster set.

T0172.text: A set with no rep target — you go until the reps stop. Plans use it on a final set to autoregulate: how many you get tells you whether the load is right, without the plan having to guess your exact strength on the day.

T0173.text: Log what you actually got. That number is what the app reads for ${term("overload","progression")}.

T0174.text: Taken until another rep is genuinely not there.

T0175.text: That's ${term("rpe","RPE")} 10 — not "it got hard", but a rep you attempted and could not finish. It buys a little extra stimulus per set and costs a lot more recovery, which is why most plans reserve it for the last set of an exercise, and why Element 26's ${term("mrv","MRV")} estimate drops when your average RPE climbs.

T0177.text: How long to wait depends on how hard the set was, not one number for everything.

T0179.text: Heavy sets, 6 reps or fewer, or anything at ${term("rpe","RPE")} 9.5+. Your strength systems genuinely take this long to reload.

T0181.text: Normal 8-12 rep work. The bulk of what you do.

T0183.text: High-rep and finisher work, where recovery is fast.

T0184.text: Cutting rest short doesn't make a workout more productive, it just makes the next set lighter, which quietly caps the ${term("volume","volume")} you accumulate. If you're short on time, it's better to drop an exercise than to rush the ones you keep.

T0185.text: Element 26 starts the stopwatch when you tap ✓, works out which band that set was in, and asks you to confirm if you stop the clock well before you should.

T0187.text: How many reps you lose from your first set to your last at the same weight.

T0188.text: Losing some is completely normal, around 25% across three sets is typical and healthy. Getting 10, then 9, then 8 means you judged the weight well.

T0189.text: A steep drop, 12 then 6, almost always means one of two things: your ${term("restwindow","rest was too short")}, or your first set was too heavy and taken too close to ${term("failure","failure")}. Both leave your later sets contributing fatigue without much stimulus.

T0190.text: The fix is usually to start about 5 lb lighter and hold the reps, which nets more total quality work than one heroic first set followed by two poor ones.

T0192.text: How many working sets you get through per hour.

T0193.text: Roughly 15-20 sets an hour is a brisk, focused session. Much under 12 usually means long gaps that aren't real ${term("restwindow","rest")}, phone, queuing for equipment, wandering.

T0194.text: Density isn't a goal in itself; the point is that a 90-minute session that could have been 55 costs you the same ${term("volume","volume")} for far more of your life, and set quality falls off past about 80 minutes anyway.

T0196.text: A set is not worth the same to every muscle it touches, so it is not counted as if it were.

T0197.text: A dumbbell bench press counts as a full set for your chest, about half a set for your front shoulders, and about half for your triceps. Those muscles genuinely worked, but not nearly as hard as the chest did, and counting all three as full sets would make your weekly totals roughly triple what you actually did.

T0198.text: Six things decide the weight a muscle gets from an exercise:

T0200.text: How hard the muscle actually fires. EMG research consistently shows the target muscle working far harder than its assistants on the same lift.

T0202.text: A muscle taken through a full stretch under load grows more than one working in a short range. This is why an overhead extension is worth more to the ${term("mev","triceps long head")} than a pushdown: only the overhead position actually lengthens it.

T0204.text: If you are fighting to balance, the target muscle cannot be driven as hard. A machine row loads the lats more precisely than a bent-over row at the same effort.

T0206.text: Compound lifts drain you systemically, not just locally. Ten sets of squats and ten of leg extensions do not cost the same, which is why the ${term("mrv","MRV")} calculation cares about your compound share.

T0208.text: Movements you can reliably add weight to week after week drive more growth over time than ones that stall or where form breaks down first.

T0210.text: Where research gives a clear answer it wins over feel. Seated versus standing calf raises is the cleanest example: knee bent hits the ${term("mev","soleus")}, knee straight hits the gastrocnemius, and no amount of effort swaps them.

T0211.text: The practical upshot: if a muscle only ever shows up as a fraction, it has no direct work in your programme. Assisting on other people's lifts is not the same as being trained.

T0213.text: Two different things get called "volume". Element 26 uses both, in different places.

T0215.text: The unit for ${term("mev","MEV")} / ${term("mav","MAV")} / ${term("mrv","MRV")} and everything on the Body tab. This is what the research on how much to train is expressed in.

T0217.text: weight × reps × sets, the "lb moved" figure in History and your cycle wrapped. Good for a sense of scale, poor for planning, it makes high-rep leg work look enormous next to heavy pressing.

T0218.text: When you see a volume judgement in this app, under-stimulated, in range, over MRV, it's always counting ${term("hardset","hard sets")}, never tonnage.

T0220.text: RIR is how many more reps you could have done when you stopped. It is the same idea as ${term("rpe","RPE")}, counted the other way up.

T0221.text:
RIR 0  → nothing left, that's ${term("failure","failure")}
RIR 1  → one more rep was in you
RIR 2  → two more
RIR 3  → three more, comfortably short

T0222.text: The conversion is just subtraction: RPE = 10 − RIR. A plan written in "2 RIR" and a plan written in "RPE 8" are asking for exactly the same set.

T0223.text: Why it matters. Most of the growth in a set comes from the reps near your limit, and most of the fatigue comes from the ones past it. Stopping one to three short is where that trade is best for nearly everyone.

T0225.text: Hypertrophy is muscle getting bigger. It's the goal most people mean by "building muscle", as opposed to purely getting stronger at a lift.

T0226.text: In practice it asks for moderate reps (roughly 6-20), enough sets per muscle per week, and sets taken close enough to your limit to count as ${term("hardset","hard sets")} — then a little more over time, which is ${term("overload","progressive overload")}.

T0227.text: Why it matters here. A plan aimed at size is judged on volume per muscle, which is what the Body tab measures. A plan aimed at strength would be judged on load instead, and would look "under-trained" on the same screen while working perfectly well.

T0229.text: Unilateral means one limb at a time: a single-arm row, a split squat, a one-leg curl. Bilateral is both together — a barbell squat, a bench press.

T0230.text: It matters for logging, because a set of a one-limb movement is a set for ONE side. Element 26 can mark each set L or R and alternate down the sets, so three sets runs right, left, right — which also means an odd set count is not equal work per side within a session.

T0231.text: It matters for training, because sides drift apart quietly. Tracking them separately is the only way to notice, and matching the weaker side is one way to close a gap once you have.

T0233.text: Bilateral means both limbs at once: a barbell bench press, a squat, a pulldown. The opposite is ${term("unilateral","unilateral")} work, one limb at a time.

T0234.text: Nothing special happens to a bilateral movement here — one set is one set, and no sides are marked. It is worth knowing the word only because plans use it to say which of the two they mean.

T2201.text: • isTrainingPlan — is this a training programme, as opposed to a nutrition sheet, an invoice, a class timetable, a medical form, an article about training, a race schedule, a blank template with no content, or anything else?

T2212.text: You transcribe a person's existing weight-training programme into structured JSON for a training-log app called Element 26. The input may be pasted text, a spreadsheet, a coach's PDF, a screenshot, or a photograph of a handwritten sheet.

T2213.text: YOUR ONE JOB IS TRANSCRIPTION. Everything you output must be traceable to something the document says. You are not writing a programme, improving one, or filling in what a good coach would have written. Where the document is silent, SAY NOTHING — leave the field out, leave the array empty, and set the matching flag in 'stated' to false. The app asks the person about anything you leave open, which is always better than you guessing on their behalf.

T2214.text: 1. One entry in 'days' is ONE TRAINING SESSION in the rotation, in the order it is performed. Do not create a day for rest. If the source names its sessions (Push, Pull, Upper A, Chest and Triceps, Day 1), keep those names exactly.

T2215.text: 2. If the programme repeats the same sessions every week, describe those sessions once. Put week-to-week differences in 'weeklyChanges' rather than inventing extra days.

T2216.text: 3b. 'restDaysFlexible' true ONLY where the document says in as many words that the rest days are the lifter's to place \u2014 'take rest days as needed', 'train 4 days a week, any days you like', 'schedule the off days to suit you'. A plan that simply never mentions rest days is NOT saying this: leave it false. Naming fixed days (\u2018Mon/Wed/Fri\u2019) or writing rest into the rotation is the opposite of flexible.

T2217.text: 3c. 'daysAnyOrder' true ONLY where the document says the SESSIONS themselves may be performed in any order \u2014 'do these in whatever order suits your week', 'the three workouts can be done on any days'. Listing sessions as Day 1, Day 2, Day 3, or as Push then Pull then Legs, is prescribing an order, not permitting any: leave it false. Silence is false.

T2218.text: 4b. 'planKind' IS THE ONE PLACE YOU MAY READ BETWEEN THE LINES, and it is fenced. Everything else in this schema is transcription; this is a classification, and the app needs it to know what somebody is actually running. Fill it in from the sessions themselves: a Push / Pull / Legs rotation is family 'ppl' whether or not those words appear, four sessions alternating upper and lower body is 'upper_lower', one session per muscle group is 'bro_split'. 'named' is different and much stricter: put a published programme's name there ONLY if the document names it — 5/3/1, StrongLifts 5x5, PHUL, PHAT, GZCLP, nSuns, Starting Strength, Candito, Sheiko — and leave it empty if the plan merely resembles one, because 'this looks like 5/3/1' is a guess and the app will show it to the person as a fact. Set 'stated' true only when the document says in words what kind of plan it is, false when you worked it out from the structure, and put what you worked it out FROM in 'evidence' — a heading, a sentence, or 'sessions named Push, Pull, Legs'. Where the shape genuinely does not resolve, 'unclear' is a real answer and a better one than a confident wrong label.

T2219.text: 4. 'weeks' is how many weeks the programme runs, if it says. 'goal' ONLY if the document says what it is for — a title like "12-Week Hypertrophy Block" or a line saying it is a strength or fat-loss programme counts; a plan that merely looks like one does not. Otherwise 'unstated'.

T2220.text: 5. 'sets' is the number of working sets as the document writes them. If it prescribes sets PER SIDE ('3 sets each arm'), put 3 and set setsArePerSide true. Do not double it yourself — the app doubles it or not depending on how the person chooses to track sides.

T2221.text: 6. 'reps' is exactly as prescribed, as a short string: '8', '6-10', '12-15', 'AMRAP', '30s', '20 each leg'. Never a sentence. If the document gives no rep target at all, use an empty string.

T2222.text: 7. 'rpe' or 'rir' ONLY if the document gives them, one per set in order. Never invent effort targets and never convert one into a guess. If the document says 'last set to failure' or 'leave 2 in the tank on the top set', put that in effortNote and leave the numeric arrays empty.

T2223.text: 8. REST. Fill 'restSeconds' on EVERY exercise the document prescribes a rest for, including when it is prescribed once for all of them. Plans very often state rest ONCE, at the top or under a day heading — 'Rest 2-3 min between sets', 'rest 90s', '2 min compounds / 60s isolation', 'Rest as needed on the main lifts' — and that is a rest for every exercise it covers, not an absence of one. Read it, and write the number onto each exercise it applies to. Where a rule names categories, apply it per category: 'compounds' means the multi-joint lifts of that session, 'isolation' or 'accessories' the single-joint ones. Where a rest is stated for the whole plan or a whole day AS WELL as on individual rows, the row wins for that row. Give a range as its LOW number ('2-3 min' is restSeconds 120) and put the words in restNote. Also set 'defaultRestSeconds' at the top level, and 'restSeconds' on a day, whenever the document states a blanket rest at that level — even after you have already copied it onto the exercises. Only omit all of it if the document genuinely never mentions rest.
